# Introduction

The anthropogenic climate crisis is a significant threat to global health [@vanDaalen2022].
The health-care sector is responsible for an estimated 5–10% of greenhouse gas emissions [@Hu2021].
Fluorinated volatile anaesthetics such as sevoflurane and desflurane are a relevant source of these emissions [@MacNeill2017; @Hu2021].
As per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, they also give rise to persistent degradation products
that accumulate in aquatic ecosystems,
representing an environmental risk beyond their greenhouse warming potential [@Kalmar2025b].

Activated carbon canisters fitted passively at the exhaust port of the anaesthesia workstation
can adsorb exhaled volatile anaesthetics and reduce their atmospheric release [@Gibb2024b].
The CONTRAfluran^TM^ canister (ZeoSys Medical GmbH, Berlin, Germany)
is the only system currently approved in Europe for pharmaceutical reuse of recaptured sevoflurane,
recovering a usable pharmaceutical product rather than merely destroying captured emissions.

Published evidence on CONTRAfluran capture efficiency for sevoflurane is limited.
Mulier et al. reported an *in vivo* mass transfer of 45% during laparoscopic surgery
without quantifying the overall recapture rate [@Mulier2024a].
A preceding single-centre study found a 34% recapture rate with CONTRAfluran
across two operating rooms under routine conditions [@Gibb2025].

Multicentre data, which could reduce site-specific bias and improve generalisability, remain lacking [@Gandhi2024].
We therefore conducted a prospective, multicentre, international observational study
across `r n_center["initial"]` hospitals in Germany and Austria
to quantify the proportion of sevoflurane recaptured by CONTRAfluran under routine clinical conditions
and to explore clinical predictors of per-canister capture efficiency.
